newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's Van der Horst in satellite deal.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's Van der Horst in satellite deal.

text.p: Engineering group Van der Horst Ltd (VDH) has invested in a satellite company Space Imaging to boost its long term income and is negotiating distribution rights in Asia, chairman Johannes Kotjo said on Tuesday.

"The most important is the additional recurrent income for Van der Horst. You are talking about a 35 to 40 percent IRR (internal rate of return)," Kotjo told reporters at a news conference to announce the venture.
The company expects the deal to generate contributions to its income from 1999, he said.
Singapore-based VDH said on Tuesday it was investing US$25 million in U.S.-based Space Imaging through its subsidiary Van der Horst - SI Ltd.
VDH would have a nine percent stake in Space Imaging whose original partners were Lockheed Martin Corp, Raytheon E-Systems and Mitsubishi Corp.
Kotjo said VDH had the option to raise its stake in Space Imaging to 20 percent and it was likely to do so.
Space Imaging is launching the world's first commercial one-metre resolution imaging satellite in December 1997 and a second is planned for September 1998.
The satellites will provide high quality, high resolution space imagery of the earth to markets such as utilities, agriculture, transport, resource management and geographic information systems.

The partners have together invested half of the cost of launching both satellites, estimated at US$500 million, said John Copple, Space Imaging's chief executive officer. The remaining cost is funded by debt, he said.
"We will start producing profits in 1998. The (net) profit in the first year ... between US$100-$200 million. The profits (will) double every year for about three years," said Copple.
Space Imaging is building its customer base and saw revenue of US$200-$300 million in the early years from 1998, rising to US$1.0 billion over a five-year period, he said.
Space Imaging currently sells space imagery from the Indian IRS-1C satellite. It plans to launch more satellites around the year 2000 and VDH will remain its partner, he added.

Kotjo said VDH was negotiating for imaging distribution rights in the Asian region, which would give it additional income. The distribution area would probably encompass Indochina and the ASEAN countries, except Thailand.
ASEAN is the Association of Southeast Asian Nations comprising Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Philippines, Indonesia, Brunei and Vietnam.
If successful, VDH would build an earth station in Asia costing around US$20 million. VDH could sell equity stakes in the earth station but would operate it, Kotjo said.
He saw organisations like the World Bank, infrastructure companies, forestry and agricultural industries and television service companies as potential customers in the region.
